briefs.learning_objective: Compute the mean, median, and mode of a dataset and choose which one best represents its typical (central) value, especially when the data is skewed.

required_facts.statement: The sample mean is computed as the sum of the observed values divided by the number of observations.
The median is the middle value when the data are ordered from smallest to largest; if there is an even number of observations, the median is the average of the two middle values.
The mode is the value that occurs most often in the data; there can be more than one mode.

The mean is more strongly affected by extreme observations (such as those in the tail of a skewed distribution) than the median, which is more robust to them; for this reason the median can better represent a typical value in a skewed dataset.

optional_enrichment.statement: A mode is a prominent peak in a distribution: a value or narrow range of values where observations are noticeably more concentrated than in neighboring regions.

briefs.learning_objective: Compute the range, variance, and standard deviation of a dataset and interpret what each says about how spread out the data are.

required_facts.statement: The range of a data set is the largest value minus the smallest value.

The variance is computed by taking each observation's deviation from the mean, squaring it, summing the squared deviations, and dividing by n - 1 (one less than the number of observations); it is roughly the average squared distance of the observations from the mean.
The standard deviation is the square root of the variance, and it describes the typical distance of an observation from the mean.

The standard deviation is expressed in the same units as the original data, while the variance is expressed in squared units; the range is based only on the two most extreme values and ignores how the rest of the data are spread.

briefs.learning_objective: Describe a distribution's shape as symmetric, right-skewed, or left-skewed, and explain what that shape implies about how the mean and median compare.

required_facts.statement: A distribution is right-skewed when it has a longer tail trailing off to the right, and left-skewed when it has a longer tail trailing off to the left.
A distribution is symmetric when it trails off by roughly equal amounts in both directions.
The mean is more affected by extreme observations, such as those in the long tail of a skewed distribution, than the median, which is more robust to them.

optional_enrichment.statement: A distribution can have one prominent peak (unimodal), two (bimodal), or more than two (multimodal).

briefs.learning_objective: Identify individual observations in a dataset that are outliers and reason about what could plausibly explain them.

required_facts.statement: An outlier is an observation that appears extreme relative to the rest of the data.
Examining a dataset for outliers can help identify strong skew in the distribution, spot possible data collection or data entry errors, and reveal interesting properties of the data.
Examine an outlier to judge whether it is a possible data collection or data entry error or a genuine observation; a genuine outlier should not be removed without a very good reason.

misconceptions.statement: An outlier is not automatically a data error: it may instead be a genuine, correct observation.

briefs.learning_objective: Read a histogram or frequency table and describe what it shows about a dataset's distribution, including its modal range and any visible skew.

required_facts.statement: A histogram groups numerical values into bins and represents the count of observations in each bin as a bar; taller bars show where the data values are relatively more common.
A mode appears in a histogram as a prominent peak: a bin, or region of neighboring bins, where observations are noticeably more concentrated than elsewhere.
The table of counts of observations in each bin, which a histogram displays as bars, is called a frequency table.

briefs.learning_objective: Given a correlation coefficient value for two numeric variables, read its sign and magnitude to state the direction and relative strength of their linear relationship.

required_facts.statement: Correlation, which always takes values between -1 and 1, describes the strength of the linear relationship between two numeric variables.

In a positive association, higher values of one variable tend to go with higher values of the other; in a negative association, higher values of one variable tend to go with lower values of the other.

A correlation near +1 indicates a strong positive linear relationship, a correlation near -1 indicates a strong negative linear relationship, and a correlation near 0 indicates little or no linear relationship.

optional_enrichment.statement: A correlation is exactly -1 or 1 only when the relationship between the two variables is perfectly linear.

misconceptions.statement: Correlation quantifies the strength of a linear relationship only; a nonlinear relationship can be strong even when its correlation value looks weak.

briefs.learning_objective: Compare several correlation coefficients to identify the strongest and weakest relationships, and explain why a strong pairwise correlation alone does not rule out a confounding variable.

required_facts.statement: The strength of a correlation is judged by its magnitude (absolute value): the closer the value is to 1, the stronger the linear relationship, regardless of whether the sign is positive or negative.

A confounding variable is a variable that is correlated with both of two other variables being studied, so it can produce an association between those two variables that is not a direct link between them.

briefs.learning_objective: Apply the correlation-vs-causation caveat when interpreting a business finding, flagging and rewriting claims that overstate what a correlational finding supports.

required_facts.statement: Association does not imply causation: a correlation between two variables does not by itself establish that one causes the other.
When only observational (correlational) data supports a finding, it should be restated as an association, or as a hypothesis to check later, rather than as a causal claim.

briefs.learning_objective: Describe pandas' Series and DataFrame structures and how they relate, and construct a Series from a list and a DataFrame from a dict of lists.

required_facts.statement: A pandas Series is a one-dimensional labeled array that can hold data of any type; its axis labels are collectively called the index.
A pandas DataFrame is a two-dimensional labeled data structure whose columns can hold different types, and it can be thought of as a dict of Series objects that share an index.

A pandas Series can be constructed from data that is array-like, an Iterable (such as a Python list), a dict, or a scalar value. When built from a list (or other array-like data) with no index passed, the index defaults to 0, 1, ..., len(data) - 1; when built from a dict, the dict's keys become the index.
A DataFrame can be constructed from a dict of equal-length lists, where each key becomes a column name and each list becomes that column's values.
A DataFrame can be treated like a dict of like-indexed Series: df['col'] gets a column, and df['new'] = ... sets (or adds) a column, using the same syntax as the analogous dict operations.

briefs.learning_objective: Load tabular data from a CSV or Excel file into a DataFrame using read_csv or read_excel.

required_facts.statement: read_csv() is the main pandas function for reading a delimited text file, such as a CSV file, into a DataFrame.
read_excel() reads an Excel file (such as a .xlsx workbook) into a DataFrame.
read_csv() takes the file path (or URL) to read as its first argument, and read_excel() additionally takes a sheet_name argument to choose which sheet of the workbook to load.
read_csv() accepts arguments such as sep to change the field delimiter used to parse the file (the default is a comma).

briefs.learning_objective: Construct a DataFrame directly from Python data, such as a dict of lists or a list of dicts, rather than loading it from a file.

required_facts.statement: A DataFrame can be constructed from a dict of equal-length lists, where each key becomes a column name and each list becomes that column's values; if no index is passed, the result uses a default range index.
A DataFrame can also be constructed from a list of dicts, where each dict becomes one row and the dict keys become the column names.

briefs.learning_objective: Get an initial overview of a newly-loaded DataFrame using head, info, describe, shape, and dtypes.

required_facts.statement: head() (and tail()) shows a small sample of the first (or last) rows of a Series or DataFrame; by default it shows five rows.
The shape attribute reports a DataFrame's axis dimensions: the number of rows and the number of columns.
The dtypes attribute returns the data type of each column in a DataFrame.
info() prints a concise summary of a DataFrame, including its columns and their data types, how many non-missing values each column has, and its memory usage.
describe() computes a quick statistical overview of a Series' values, or of each numeric column of a DataFrame, in a single call.

briefs.learning_objective: Compute descriptive statistics for a DataFrame column using pandas methods such as describe, mean, median, and std.

required_facts.statement: pandas provides built-in statistical methods for a Series or DataFrame column, including mean() (mean of values), median() (arithmetic median), and std() (sample standard deviation).
describe() computes a set of summary statistics, such as count, mean, std, min, quartiles, and max, for a Series or for each numeric column of a DataFrame in one call.

briefs.learning_objective: Select rows and columns from a DataFrame by label using loc, or by integer position using iloc.

required_facts.statement: .loc selects data primarily by label (row or column names), while .iloc selects data primarily by integer position, from 0 to length-1 of the axis.
.loc slicing with labels (e.g. 'a':'f') includes both the start and the stop labels in the result, unlike ordinary Python slicing where the stop is excluded.
.iloc uses 0-based positional indexing where, when slicing, the start position is included and the stop position is excluded, following ordinary Python/NumPy slicing rules.

Both .loc and .iloc select using a row selector and a column selector separated by a comma (e.g. df.loc[rows, cols]); an axis left out of the selection, or given as a colon (:), means 'all of that axis', so df.loc['a'] is equivalent to df.loc['a', :].

briefs.learning_objective: Filter DataFrame rows using a boolean condition on a column.

required_facts.statement: You may select rows from a DataFrame using a boolean vector the same length as the DataFrame's index; only the rows where the vector is True are kept.

Comparing a DataFrame column with a value (e.g. df['A'] > 0) produces a True/False Series of the same length as the column, which can be used directly inside the DataFrame's [] to keep only the matching rows (e.g. df[df['A'] > 0]).

When combining multiple boolean conditions with the operators | (or), & (and), or ~ (not), each condition must be grouped in parentheses, because Python would otherwise evaluate the comparison operators in an unintended order.

briefs.learning_objective: Sort a DataFrame by the values in one or more columns, in ascending or descending order.

required_facts.statement: DataFrame.sort_values(by=...) sorts rows using the values of the listed column(s); when by is a list of column names, the first column sets the primary sort order and each later column breaks ties among rows that were equal in the previous column(s).
sort_values()'s ascending parameter defaults to True, and can be given as a list of booleans matching the length of by, to sort some columns ascending and others descending in the same call.

optional_enrichment.statement: pandas supports sorting by index labels using sort_index(), and sorting by column values using sort_values().

briefs.learning_objective: Rename a DataFrame's column labels and/or index labels using rename.

required_facts.statement: The rename() method relabels a DataFrame's axes using a dict or Series mapping (or a function); passing a columns= mapping renames column labels and an index= mapping renames row index labels.
A single rename() call can rename columns and index labels together by passing both the columns and index arguments at once; any label not included in the mapping is left unchanged.

briefs.learning_objective: Convert a DataFrame column's dtype to a different, correct dtype using astype.

required_facts.statement: The astype() method explicitly converts a column's (or Series') values from one dtype to another, returning a copy by default, and it raises an exception if the requested conversion is invalid.
astype() can convert a single column, a subset of a DataFrame's columns at once, or specific columns to specific dtypes by passing a dict mapping column names to target dtypes.

briefs.learning_objective: Convert a column of date-like text to pandas datetime values with to_datetime, and extract date components using the .dt accessor.

required_facts.statement: The to_datetime() function converts a Series (or list-like) of date-like strings or other date-like values into pandas datetime values; when passed a Series, it returns a Series with the same index.
Once a column has a datetime dtype, its .dt accessor exposes date/time component properties, such as year, month, and day, for each value.

briefs.learning_objective: Clean and transform a text column using the .str accessor's vectorized string methods, such as strip, lower, and replace.

required_facts.statement: A Series' .str accessor lets you call ordinary string-processing methods, matching the names of Python's built-in string methods (such as lower, strip, and replace), on every element of the Series at once.

optional_enrichment.statement: The .str accessor's methods automatically exclude missing/NA values when applying the operation.

briefs.learning_objective: Remove duplicate rows from a DataFrame using drop_duplicates, based on the correct columns and the intended occurrence to keep.

required_facts.statement: duplicated() returns a boolean vector indicating which rows are duplicates, and drop_duplicates() removes duplicate rows; both take as an argument the columns used to identify a duplicated row.

By default, drop_duplicates() keeps the first occurrence of each duplicate set and drops the rest; passing keep='last' keeps the last occurrence instead, and keep=False drops every row that is part of a duplicate set.

briefs.learning_objective: Detect, drop, or fill missing values in a DataFrame using isna, dropna, and fillna.

required_facts.statement: isna() (and its complement notna()) detects which values in a Series or DataFrame are missing.
dropna() removes rows that contain missing values; passing a subset of column labels restricts which columns are checked when deciding whether a row counts as having a missing value.
fillna() replaces missing (NA) values with a specified value, such as a scalar (for example, replacing every missing value in a column with 0).

optional_enrichment.statement: isna() (and its complement notna()) also treat None as a missing value.

briefs.learning_objective: Substitute or translate the values of a pandas Series element-wise using .map() with a function or a mapping.

required_facts.statement: Series.map() accepts a Python function taking a single value and returning a single value, and applies it to every element of the Series.
Series.map() can substitute each value in the Series using a mapping correspondence that may be a function, a dict, or a Series.

briefs.learning_objective: Transform DataFrame or Series values by applying a custom function along an axis using .apply().

required_facts.statement: DataFrame.apply() applies an arbitrary function along an axis of the DataFrame, operating on each column by default, or on each row when axis=1.

optional_enrichment.statement: For element-wise work, pandas provides map() (Series.map, or DataFrame.map for a whole DataFrame) rather than apply().

briefs.learning_objective: Stack multiple DataFrames with the same structure along rows or columns using concat.

required_facts.statement: pd.concat() concatenates multiple Series or DataFrame objects along an axis.
By default, pd.concat() stacks the given DataFrames row-wise, appending each one's rows below the previous, producing one combined DataFrame when they share the same columns.
pd.concat() takes an axis parameter: by default (no axis argument), it stacks the objects row-wise, while axis=1 places them side by side as columns.

optional_enrichment.statement: pd.concat() can also perform a union or intersection of the indexes on the other (non-stacking) axis, controlled by its join parameter.
Passing ignore_index=True to pd.concat() discards the original row labels and renumbers the combined result starting from 0.

briefs.learning_objective: Combine two related DataFrames on a shared key column using merge, with the correct join type.

required_facts.statement: merge() combines two DataFrames by matching values in a shared key column, which can be specified with the on parameter.
The how parameter to merge() controls which keys are kept in the result; how='inner' (the default) keeps only the key values present in both DataFrames.
If a key value does not appear in one of the two DataFrames being merged, the corresponding values contributed by that DataFrame in the joined result are NA.
The how parameter also accepts 'left' (keep all keys from the left DataFrame only), 'right' (keep all keys from the right DataFrame only), and 'outer' (keep the union of keys from both DataFrames).

briefs.learning_objective: Split a DataFrame into groups by a key, apply an aggregation, and combine the results into one summarized row per group using groupby.

required_facts.statement: Group by refers to a process involving one or more of the following steps: splitting the data into groups based on some criteria, applying a function to each group independently, and combining the results into a data structure.
An aggregation is a groupby operation that reduces each group to a single summary value per column, such as computing the sum of a column within each group.

In practice, you call df.groupby(key) and then an aggregation method such as .sum() or .mean() on the DataFrame or a selected column, or .agg([...]) to compute several aggregations at once; by default the group keys become the index of the result.

briefs.learning_objective: Reshape a wide-format DataFrame into long format using melt.

required_facts.statement: melt() reshapes a DataFrame from wide to long format: the columns listed as id_vars stay as identifier columns, while all other columns are unpivoted into two columns, one holding the original column names and one holding their values.
The default 'variable' and 'value' column names produced by melt() can be renamed using its var_name and value_name parameters.

briefs.learning_objective: Reshape long-format data into a wide summary table using pivot_table.

required_facts.statement: pivot_table() reshapes data by turning the distinct values of one column into new columns, and unlike plain pivot(), it can handle duplicate index/column combinations by aggregating the numeric values.
pivot_table() takes index, columns, and values arguments: index sets the rows of the output table, columns sets the new columns, and values selects which column(s) to aggregate into the table.
pivot_table() combines rows that share the same index/column values using aggfunc, which defaults to 'mean'; passing aggfunc='sum' (or another function) changes how those values are combined.

briefs.learning_objective: Export a cleaned DataFrame to a CSV file using to_csv, with or without writing the index column as required.

required_facts.statement: The to_csv() method on a Series or DataFrame writes its contents to a CSV file; the destination path or buffer is its only required argument.
to_csv()'s index argument controls whether the row (index) labels are written to the file; it defaults to True, and passing index=False omits them.
